subject: Computer Networking
title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: A quick win: understand Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

hook.text: An attacker injects JavaScript into a trusted website. When you visit, the script runs in your browser.

buildup.text: Stored XSS saves malicious code in a database. Every user who views the page gets attacked.

discovery.text: Reflected XSS hides the script in a URL. Click the link and the server echoes the attack back to you.

twist.text: XSS steals cookies, session tokens, and personal data. It's the most common web vulnerability for years.

climax.text: Content Security Policy headers restrict which scripts can run. Combined with output encoding, XSS is preventable.

punchline.text: XSS injects scripts into trusted sites. Sanitize all user input.

quiz.question: What does a Content Security Policy header help prevent?
options: Unauthorized scripts from running on the page
SQL queries from reaching the database
Users from accessing pages without logging in

details.summary: Cross-site scripting injects malicious JavaScript into web pages that other users then execute in their browsers. Stored XSS persists in databases, reflected XSS bounces off server responses, and DOM-based XSS exploits client-side scripts.
details.whyItMatters: XSS is one of the most prevalent web vulnerabilities. It can steal session cookies, redirect users, and perform actions as the victim. Understanding XSS prevention is essential for secure web development.
takeaways: XSS injects malicious scripts that execute in victim browsers
Output encoding converts special characters to harmless text
Content Security Policy restricts which scripts can execute

faq.question: What is the difference between stored and reflected XSS?
faq.answer: Stored XSS saves the malicious script in the server's database, like a comment field, attacking every user who views the page. Reflected XSS includes the script in a URL parameter that the server echoes back.

faq.question: How does Content Security Policy prevent XSS?
faq.answer: CSP tells browsers which sources of scripts are trusted. A policy like script-src 'self' only allows scripts from the site's own origin. Inline scripts are blocked by default unless explicitly allowed with hashes or nonces.
